extracted.intended_audience: labor and employment lawyers, employers and their counsel, unions and employee representatives, HR professionals, franchisors/franchisees, and rulemaking commenters/participants
extracted.subtask_description: Final-rule guidance from the National Labor Relations Board defining when two or more entities are joint employers under the NLRA, specifying required common-law foundations, precise definitions (including a closed list of essential terms), evidentiary rules, bargaining obligations, and severability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding in common-law agency principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The joint-employer analysis is based on common-law agency principles; the Board looks to judicial articulations and secondary compendiums and focuses on established common-law definitions at the time Congress enacted the NLRA (1935) and the Taft-Hartley Amendments (1947).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may not depart from common-law agency principles for the sake of predicted effects on particular industries; courts' and compendia's formulations of the common law are primary guidance. The Board incorporates decisions like BFI and related appellate guidance in interpreting common-law concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer of particular employees (Section 103.40(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'employer' for purposes of particular employees exists where the employer has an employment relationship with those employees under common-law agency principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing a common-law employment relationship is a necessary prerequisite to any joint-employer finding; the Board evaluates this threshold using common-law indicia from judicial authority and secondary sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Joint Employers (Section 103.40(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more employers of the same particular employees are joint employers if the employers share or codetermine matters governing employees' essential terms and conditions of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test applies across contexts under the Act (representation and unfair-labor-practice contexts) and codifies the longstanding core of the joint-employer test consistent with court formulations (e.g., Third Circuit, D.C. Circuit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'share or codetermine' (Section 103.40(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Share or codetermine those matters governing employees' essential terms and conditions of employment' means possessing the authority to control (directly or indirectly) or exercising the power to control (directly or indirectly) one or more essential terms and conditions of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of authority or reserved right to control and evidence of exercise of control (including indirect control through an intermediary) is probative. The definition incorporates BFI reasoning that both authority and exercise (direct or indirect) matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed list of essential terms and conditions of employment (Section 103.40(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule defines 'essential terms and conditions of employment' by an exclusive, closed list of seven categories: (1) wages, benefits, and other compensation; (2) hours of work and scheduling; (3) assignment of duties to be performed; (4) supervision of the performance of duties; (5) work rules and directions governing the manner, means, and methods of performance and grounds for discipline; (6) the tenure of employment, including hiring and discharge; and (7) working conditions related to safety and health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These seven categories represent the core subjects of collective bargaining; only control over matters falling into these categories can serve as the object of control necessary to establish joint-employer status. The closed list aims to ensure bargaining will be meaningful and to prevent joint-employer findings based on peripheral or attenuated matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control sufficient to establish joint-employer status (Section 103.40(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessing the authority to control one or more essential terms and conditions of employment is sufficient to establish joint-employer status regardless of whether the control is actually exercised; exercising the power to control indirectly (including through an intermediary) is likewise sufficient regardless of direct exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The relevant object of control must be an 'essential' term as defined in §103.40(d). This provision aims to prevent reliance on attenuated, insubstantial, or unexercised control over peripheral matters and clarifies that reserved authority and indirect exercise can establish status under common-law principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect control and unexercised authority are probative
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect control (including control exerted through an intermediary) and unexercised/reserved authority to control are probative evidence of joint-employer status under common-law agency principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and Board precedent recognize that unexercised authority and indirect control can establish an employment or joint-employer relationship; the Board rejects requiring actual exercise of control as necessary. The rule incorporates appellate guidance (e.g., D.C. Circuit's criticism of ignoring indirect control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control immaterial to joint-employer status (Section 103.40(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of an entity's control over matters that are immaterial to the existence of an employment relationship under common-law agency principles and that do not bear on employees' essential terms and conditions is not relevant to whether the entity is a joint employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This excludes kinds of control commonly embodied in true independent-contractor contracts and distinguishes ordinary indirect control intrinsic to third-party contracting from indirect control over essential terms of employment; helps prevent overbroad joint-employer findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof (Section 103.40(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party asserting that an employer is a joint employer of particular employees bears the burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allocation is consistent with the 2020 rule, BFI, and prior precedent; claimants must meet the preponderance standard to establish joint-employer status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bargaining obligations of a joint employer (Section 103.40(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint employer must bargain collectively with the employees' representative with respect to any term and condition of employment that it possesses the authority to control or exercises the power to control, regardless of whether that term is an 'essential' term; conversely, it is not required to bargain about terms it does not control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that bargaining obligations extend beyond the closed list of 'essential' terms to any ordinary mandatory subject of bargaining the joint employer controls, ensuring collective bargaining is meaningful. Also clarifies that where multiple entities each control terms, an employer need not bargain over matters not subject to its control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of workplace health and safety as an essential term
rubrics_metrics.description: Working conditions related to the safety and health of employees are included among the essential terms and conditions of employment; authority or discretion over workplace health and safety supports a joint-employer finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely memorializing compliance with legal health and safety obligations does not by itself make an entity a joint employer; entities exercising discretion over workplace health and safety are properly treated as joint employers because bargaining over these matters is central to employees' collective rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability (Section 103.40(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions and subprovisions of the final rule are intended to be severable; if any part is held unlawful, the remainder is intended to remain in effect to the fullest extent permitted by law. The rescission of the 2020 Rule is intended to be severable from the final rule's terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board states its intent to preserve as much of the rule as a reviewing body approves; this is a procedural/structural rule element rather than a substantive test but affects implementation if parts are invalidated.
